article_content: Inside a tall, red-brick building in Alexandria, Virginia, lies a federal courtroom awaiting Edward Snowden â the former NSA contractor who leaked classified intelligence. Though he currently resides in Russia under temporary asylum, the U.S. government has charged him under the Espionage Act in the Eastern District of Virginia â a court famously known as the 'rocket docket' for its rapid handling of national security cases. While no formal indictment has been issued, the speed and severity of prosecutions in this district mean Snowden must carefully consider his next steps. His one-year temporary asylum in Russia offers breathing room, but it is not permanent. Legal experts suggest he now has three realistic paths: secure long-term asylum in a friendly country like those in South America, negotiate a plea deal with U.S. authorities, or risk deportation by Russia to the U.S. or Hong Kong â both of which have extradition treaties with Washington. The U.S. has no extradition treaty with Russia, largely because lawmakers feared Russia might demand the return of its own dissidents. Meanwhile, Snowdenâs U.S. passport has been revoked, leaving him vulnerable to being forcibly returned by Russian authorities to any country that recognizes his citizenship â including the U.S. itself. Another option: seek sanctuary in a foreign embassy in Moscow. As WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange found in Londonâs Ecuadorian Embassy, embassies offer legal immunity from arrest â and the U.S. cannot enter sovereign territory to seize him. However, experts agree that a covert U.S. operation to snatch Snowden off Moscowâs streets â as seen in Hollywood films â remains highly improbable.

article_content: The United States accounts for just 5 percent of the worldâs population but incarcerates nearly a quarter of the worldâs prisoners. With 2.2 million people held in state and federal facilities, overcrowding has become so severe that the White House is open to considering unconventional solutions to reduce inmate numbers. Warden Rick Van Wickler of New Hampshireâs Cheshire County Correctional Facility believes he has found one: granting inmates unprecedented freedomsâincluding pets and, crucially, no perimeter fences. The facility, which resembles a school more than a traditional prison, houses 230 male and female inmates. Van Wickler, who spent 13 years securing funding and touring prisons nationwide to develop his model, argues that punishment alone fails to reduce recidivism. Instead, he champions rehabilitation through dignity, trust, and environmental design. Inmates and correctional officers interact freely in bright, open spaces, eliminating territorial tensions. Staff and inmates address each other by nameânot âofficerâ or âinmateââfostering mutual respect. The prison features art and craft programs, allowing inmates to discover new skills. Pets, such as a cat named Polo from the Humane Society, are cared for by female inmates until adoptionâa program praised for improving emotional well-being. Security relies not on walls or barriers but on a 24/7 network of surveillance cameras monitored in a room dubbed 'the secret squirrel room.' Solitary confinement is reserved for serious infractions and capped at 15 days. Inmates may shower or make one phone call daily during isolation and are permitted two booksâbut no radios, TVs, or photographs. Van Wickler contends that imprisoning nonviolent drug offenders is both costly and ineffective. He contrasts the approximately 70,000 annual U.S. deaths from illicit drugs with far higher fatalities from tobacco (~480,000), alcohol (~95,000), obesity (~300,000), and prescription medications (~70,000), arguing that criminalization is disproportionate. He emphasizes that the prison is also a workplace: 'There are 80 employees here. Arenât they entitled to a decent workspace? A little color?' Inmate Maria notes that even during room searches, officers neatly refold blankets instead of tossing belongingsâreflecting the facilityâs ethos of respect.

article_content: More than 350 years after being wrongfully executed for blood libel, Raphael Levy, a French Jew, has been officially exonerated and declared a martyr. In 1670, he was burned at the stake in Glatigny, Moselle, after being falsely accused of murdering a three-year-old Christian boy and using his blood for religious rituals â a baseless accusation common during the Middle Ages. On Sunday, over 100 people gathered in Glatigny to unveil a memorial plaque honoring Levyâs memory. Attendees included the president of the Consistoire, the official body representing Franceâs Jewish community. Mayor Victor Stallone declared, 'Today, we return to square one â we are reconciled. We resume normal relations with the Jewish community. Glatigny was cursed for centuries because of a ban imposed by the Jewish community following this tragedy.' In reality, it was not the Jewish community that cursed the town â but the town that ostracized Jews due to antisemitic hysteria. After the execution, Jewish travelers were forbidden from spending the night in Glatigny, a practice rooted in fear and falsehood. Blood libel accusations â the false claim that Jews murder Christian children to use their blood in religious ceremonies â originated in 12th-century England with the death of William of Norwich. These myths were repeatedly used to incite violence against Jewish communities across Europe and were later weaponized by the Nazis to justify genocide.

article_content: Meet Donald Robertson â fashion illustrator by day, Instagram sensation 'Donald Drawbertson' by night. Inspired by a bowl of leftover Christmas walnuts, he turned humble nutshells into tiny masterpieces, painting the faces of fashionâs biggest names onto their surfaces. The result? A delightfully odd new book called 'Fashion is Nuts.' Among the portraits: Anna Wintour, crowned 'Alpha Nut'; Karl Lagerfeld, dubbed 'Uber Nut'; Coco Chanel, cigarette in hand and wrapped in her signature bouclÃ© jacket; Kanye West, boldly declaring 'I AM A NUT'; and Grace Coddington, her fiery red hair rendered in bright orange duct tape. Each one is a loving, slightly absurd tribute to the wild, unapologetic spirit of fashion. Robertson, a 53-year-old dad of five from Larchmont, New York, says the idea struck him when he stared at those walnuts and thought, 'They kind of look like heads.' What followed was a basement full of painted shells, late-night photo shoots with photographer Henry Leutwyler, and an explosion of online buzz. Before long, Coletteâs Sarah Andelman reached out to collaborate â proof, he says, of how fast art can go viral in todayâs digital world. The 40-page book, printed in a limited run of just 1,000 copies, sells for $40. Robertson also released $60 posters of select 'nuts,' including Hedi Slimane, Yves Saint Laurent, and Pharrell Williams. When asked if anyone took offense, he admitted he was only nervous about capturing Pat McGrathâs famously smooth skin â so he hunted down the smoothest walnut he could find. She ended up sharing the entire book with her hundreds of thousands of Instagram followers. 'Iâm good,' he laughed. What began as a silly holiday experiment became a cultural moment â complete with its own hashtag, #fashionisnuts. Itâs not just art. Itâs a celebration of madness, imagination, and the unexpected places creativity hides.

article_content: A Sudanese government delegation is preparing to leave ongoing peace negotiations with Darfur rebels in Doha, Qatar â but officials insist theyâre not quitting the process. According to presidential advisor Ghazi Salaheldin, the delegationâs physical departure doesnât signal abandonment. He explained that even without representatives on the ground, the government remains open to reviewing any final peace draft that emerges in the coming days. Such a document, he added, would serve as the basis for a future peace conference directly in Darfur. 'We donât want peace to be blocked,' Salaheldin stressed. President Omar al-Bashir, who faces ICC charges for alleged war crimes in Darfur, had warned that talks would end if no agreement was reached by Thursday. He made clear he wonât engage with armed rebel factions after the talks conclude. 'These groups sit comfortably in foreign hotels while Darfur burns,' al-Bashir said. 'We wonât talk to anyone holding a gun and claiming to speak for the people.' In response, the Justice and Equality Movement (JEM), one of the main rebel groups, labeled al-Bashirâs remarks a direct act of aggression. Spokesperson Ahmed Hussein Adam declared the statement 'a declaration of war' that shuts the door to any political settlement. 'It kills any hope for peace,' he said. Violence erupted in Darfur in 2003 when rebel groups rose against al-Bashirâs Arab-led government. Over 300,000 lives have been lost since then, and peace efforts have repeatedly collapsed. Although the Darfur conflict is distinct from the decades-long North-South civil war, the upcoming January 9 referendum on Southern Sudanâs independence could energize rebel movements in the west, raising fears that instability may spread.

article_content: A new study reveals that British shoppers are turning away from major supermarkets, opting instead for cheaper alternatives. After a decade of steady growth fueled by rising prices, total supermarket spending has stalled since late 2013. Despite this, the volume of goods purchased has continued to rise nationally â but not within supermarkets. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) reports that spending in non-specialized food stores, primarily supermarkets, has remained virtually unchanged for over a year. Meanwhile, discount chains like Aldi and Lidl have gained significant market share, pressuring traditional players. Tesco, once the dominant force in UK grocery retail, reported a 91.9% drop in pre-tax profits over six months â its worst performance in its 95-year history. Chairman Sir Richard Broadbent stepped down shortly after the results were announced. The ONS suggests two possible reasons for falling supermarket prices: intensified competition from discounters and lower costs in food production, particularly due to declining wheat prices. Although supermarket spending has flatlined, broader retail sales remain resilient. Annual retail sales grew 2.7% in September â marking the 18th consecutive month of year-over-year growth, the longest stretch since 2008. However, recent monthly figures show a dip: retail sales volumes fell 0.3% in September, largely due to unseasonably warm weather reducing demand for winter clothing. Clothing and footwear sales dropped sharply, by 7.8% month-on-month. Petrol prices fell 5.4% year-on-year, while supermarket prices dropped 0.3% â the steepest decline since December 2004. Economists warn that this moderation in consumer spending may slow GDP growth in the coming quarters, as households face persistent weak wage growth.

article_content: Man's best friend: Researchers found having a dog can help people feel less isolated (file photo). Known as manâs best friend, dogs may also help their owners socialize more, according to a study. Researchers at the University of Chicago discovered that dog ownership is linked to reduced feelings of loneliness, while other petsâincluding cats, lizards, and hamstersâshowed no such effect. Professor John Cacioppo presented these findings at the American Association for the Advancement of Science conference: 'We find that dogs are associated with less loneliness. Unfortunately for cat owners, cats, reptiles, and rodents are not associated with a similar benefit.' He added: 'We didnât determine exactly what causes this, but one key difference is that dogs require walking. When you take them out, you get exerciseâand you meet your neighbors. Iâve met neighbors over the years through my children and my pets.' 'I think my dog also likes me, and that may be part of itâbut it might not. Simply getting out, walking, and talking to people could be enough to explain the health benefits dogs provide compared to other pets.' Chris Laurence, former veterinary director of Dogs Trust and ex-director of the Feline Advisory Bureau, noted that when dogs stop to interact, their owners often stop to chat too. 'If youâre out walking your dog, most other dog owners will say helloâat minimum. People without dogs usually just walk past,' he said. 'In terms of reducing loneliness, dogs are more of a social spur. You donât take your cat to training classes. Animals like rats are intelligent and bond with humans, but they donât prompt interactions with others.' Laurence also echoed Cacioppoâs observation about the nature of pet relationships: 'Thereâs an old sayingâyou donât own your cat; it owns you. Cats interact when they choose to. Dogs interact when you want them to.' Beyond social benefits, dogs contribute to physical health. A review by the American Heart Association suggests pet owners, especially dog owners, have healthier hearts. This may stem from increased physical activity: dog owners walk more than non-dog owners, regardless of weather. An Australian study found dog owners averaged five hours of walking per weekâcompared to fewer than three hours for those without dogs, making them more likely to meet national physical activity guidelines.

article_content: By Allan Hall. PUBLISHED: 11:21 EST, 19 September 2013. | UPDATED: 11:36 EST, 19 September 2013. Chancellor Angela Merkelâs governing coalition could face challenges as the anti-EU party AfD gains momentum, according to a recent opinion poll. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) appears poised to enter the Bundestag for the first time, after an INSA survey commissioned by the respected Bild newspaper showed growing support for the party. This shift threatens Merkelâs coalition, which has been led by her Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the smaller Free Democratic Party (FDP) since 2005. Rising AfD support reflects broader German unease over funding bailouts for struggling Southern European economiesâparticularly Greeceâand maintaining the euro at significant financial cost. Polling indicates the CDU would secure 38% of the vote and the FDP 6%, giving the coalition a combined 44%. This falls short of a parliamentary majority. The opposition blocâcenter-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), hard-left Die Linke, and the Greensâis projected to hold more seats collectively. The AfD, which advocates for repatriating powers from Brussels, is expected to reach the 5% threshold needed to win parliamentary seats. Although the SPD is unlikely to form a coalition with Die Linke, analysts warn that AfDâs entry would deprive Merkelâs coalition of a working majority. As a result, Merkel may be forced to pursue a âgrand coalitionâ with the SPD, whose support rose one percentage point to 28% in the latest poll. While the SPD has publicly resisted such a deal, experts believe it may agree under pressure. Germanyâs federal election is scheduled for Sunday.

Dressed in a crisp grey pinstripe suit, Farage didnât just celebrate â he redefined the narrative. He called his movement a 'peopleâs army' â ordinary citizens who had turned electoral frustration into power. 'Weâre getting used to this,' he said with a grin. 'And you know what? article_content: A doctor who recently returned from Guinea has tested positive for Ebola â marking the first case in New York City and the fourth diagnosed in the United States. Dr. Craig Spencer, a 33-year-old physician with Columbia Presbyterian Hospital, had been working with Doctors Without Borders in Guinea, completing his assignment on October 12. He departed Guinea on October 14 via Brussels and arrived at JFK Airport on October 17. He showed no symptoms until Thursday morning, when he developed a fever of 100.3Â°F (38Â°C), nausea, pain, and fatigue. Prior to symptom onset, he had self-monitored his temperature twice daily and avoided contact with patients. After symptoms emerged, Spencer briefly visited a Manhattan coffee stand and meatball restaurant on Tuesday, ran three miles in his neighborhood on Wednesday, and rode the subway to a bowling alley in Brooklyn on Wednesday. He was not contagious during these activities, as Ebola spreads only after symptoms appear. Health officials confirmed he was never symptomatic while using public transit. The bowling alley closed temporarily for cleaning; all locations have since been cleared by health authorities. Three individuals â his fiancÃ©e and two friends â are under quarantine and being monitored. All remain healthy, according to NYC Health Commissioner Dr. Mary Travis Bassett. The chances of transmission from Spencerâs prior contacts are 'close to nil,' she added. Spencer is now in isolation at Bellevue Hospital Center, one of eight New York hospitals designated for Ebola care. Governor Andrew Cuomo stated the state had learned from the Dallas case, where patient Thomas Eric Duncan was initially sent home and later infected two nurses. Unlike Duncan, Spencer was admitted immediately upon symptom onset. Mayor Bill de Blasio affirmed that New York followed all protocols. The CDC has deployed a team to assist. Public outreach included distributing informational flyers in Spencerâs building, clarifying Ebola transmission risks and reassuring residents that daily life remains safe. Ebola spreads only through direct contact with bodily fluids of symptomatic individuals. Spencer is the fourth person diagnosed with Ebola in the U.S. Before him, Duncan and two Texas nurses contracted the virus. Five other Americans were treated in the U.S. after being infected in West Africa â all recovered and were discharged.

article_content: A second senior Marist Church official has testified that he did not recognize intimate physical contact with a child as a crime in the 1980s â and would have sought legal advice to confirm. Alexis Turton, who led the orderâs professional standards office until 2012, told the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse that, at the time, he only knew sexual intercourse with a child was illegal. Turtonâs testimony came during proceedings involving Gregory Sutton, a former Marist Brother sentenced in 1996 for sexually abusing 67 children across New South Wales, Queensland, and the Australian Capital Territory. Just three days after learning police were investigating Sutton, Turton arranged for him to fly to Canada for âintensive therapyâ at the Southdown Clinic. Turton denied knowing the investigation had begun when he made the arrangement, insisting the move was purely therapeutic. Yet documents presented to the Commission show Sutton himself told staff in Canada that he was sent away because investigations into his abuse were underway. In 1985, Turton was informed by the principal of St Carthageâs School in Lismore that Sutton had been acting inappropriately with young girls. Turton said he was unaware Sutton had previously abused boys at a school in Far North Queensland â a fact reportedly known to that schoolâs principal and not recorded in the orderâs files. When questioned by counsel Simeon Beckett, Turton admitted he knew such acts were âvery wrong,â but claimed he would need to consult a legal expert to determine if they were criminal. He did not equate terms like âinappropriate behaviorâ with sexual assault. Turton also claimed he viewed written warnings from the school principal as industrial relations matters, not grounds for removal. Sutton was not transferred until 1987 â a decision Turton insisted was handled by another superior, Brother Alman Dwyer. Another Marist Brother, Anthony Hunt, who served as deputy principal of a school with 600 students in Lismore, similarly testified he did not understand child sexual abuse to be a crime during the 1980s. He described reports of Suttonâs conduct as âexcessive expressions of affectionâ and said he had never heard the term âpedophileâ. Commissioner Jennifer Coate pressed Hunt on whether he understood his duty to protect children. Hunt conceded he had no specific memory of media coverage on child abuse cases but maintained his perspective was shaped by the norms of the time. Turton also denied authorship of a memo referencing Suttonâs abuse history under the pseudonym âBartâ â a document Beckett argued was deliberately crafted to mislead police and potential litigants. Turton called the memo âa mysteryâ and offered no further explanation. article_content: House prices in many regions outside London have reached record highs, despite recent warnings of a market slowdown. These areas include the South East, South West, West Midlands, East of England, and Wales. Property experts say many counties still have significant room for growth. According to the Office for National Statistics, the average UK house price reached Â£272,000 in December â Â£2,000 below its peak last summer but Â£1,000 higher than the previous month. London prices remain nearly double the national average at Â£502,000, though they are still below the record high of Â£514,000 set in August. While London saw a 13% annual price increase, this is considerably slower than the 20% inflation recorded last summer. In surrounding regions, price growth is rapidly catching up: the South East rose by 12%, the East of England by 11%, and the South West by 9%. Peter Rollings of estate agent Marsh & Parsons said: 'Property prices enjoyed a rollercoaster ride in 2014. While the market has cooled from the steep accelerations of summer, it remains firmly on track, moving forward at a steadier pace. In London, where supply-demand imbalances drove prices higher, growth is still elevated but returning to normal.' Good news for aspiring homeowners: The number of mortgages granted to first-time buyers reached a seven-year high in 2014. Property prices rose in every region over the year, from a 4% increase in Wales and the North West to a 13% jump in London. As a result, a typical first-time buyer paid 10% more in December than they did a year earlier â averaging Â£208,000. For existing homeowners, the average price was Â£314,000. Campbell Robb of housing charity Shelter called the price rises 'yet another blow for millions with barely a hope of getting on the housing ladder.' Housing Minister Brandon Lewis said the government is committed to building more homes to ease pressure on prices and help hardworking people achieve homeownership. Record-low interest rates and competitive 'mortgage wars' among major lenders have aided buyers. Separately, the Council of Mortgage Lenders reported that over 300,000 mortgages â worth Â£45 billion â were issued to first-time buyers in 2014, a 15% increase from the previous year, despite stricter affordability checks introduced last year. The average age of a first-time buyer has risen to 30, up from 29 in 2007. Paul Smee, Director General of the CML, noted that improving economic conditions and government schemes like Help to Buy contributed to the highest number of first-time buyers in seven years. Help to Buy allows buyers to purchase a home with as little as a 5% deposit.

article_content: To encourage blood donations, officials in Pujiang County, Zhejiang, have launched a program that awards bonus points on high school entrance exams to students whose parents donate blood. Donors who contribute four litres receive one bonus point for their child; six litres yield two points, and eight litres grant three. To claim the reward, parents must present an official government-issued certificate verifying their donation volume. Beyond exam points, donors may also benefit from complimentary medical services, free public transportation, or modest cash incentives â all designed to make donating more attractive. One 28-year-old man, who began donating at age 18, recently reached the four-litre milestone. He shared on Weibo: 'Iâve pushed my health to the limit for this â but now my future child wonât have to worry about the exam.' Similar policies have been implemented in Baoji, Shaanxi, where citizens are encouraged â sometimes subtly pressured â to donate blood when applying for a driverâs license, registering a marriage, or starting their first job. While these measures have successfully raised donation rates, theyâve also triggered widespread online criticism. Many argue that linking altruism to personal advantage undermines its moral core. As one Weibo user remarked, 'Itâs literally a bloody policy for grades.' Others warn that turning charity into a transaction risks eroding genuine public goodwill.

article_content: (CNN) â The chilling 911 call from a man whose single-engine plane crashed into the icy Hudson River captures what he believed were his final moments. 'I am going to lose you. I am going to lose you!' Christopher Smidt, 43, told the 911 operator as he and his flight instructor exited the aircraft and entered the frigid waters of the Hudson near Yonkers, New York. 'It's freezing,' Smidt gasped as the cold overwhelmed his body. Smidt, a student pilot, and his instructor, Deniece De Priester, 39, were flying a Piper PA-32 late Sunday afternoon under visual flight rules without air traffic control services, according to the FAA. The calm 911 operator urged Smidt and De Priester to exit the cockpit: 'I need you to get out of the plane so you are not trapped inside.' 'We are out. We're not going to make it to shore,' Smidt replied over the cell phone he used to call 911. The operator assured him emergency services were en route. But Smidt remained uncertain: 'OK. I'm gonna lose you,' he said. Those were the last words the operator heard from him. Detective Daniel Higgins of the Yonkers Police Department was among the rescuers who pulled Smidt and De Priester from the water. 'We had access to pilot boats, so we were able to get aboard, start them up, and reach the two victims in the water,' he told CNN affiliate News 12 Westchester. 'If we hadn't gotten there quickly enough, well, let's just say we're glad we did.' Smidt credits De Priester for her quick thinking and skill, as well as the New York Police Department, the Yonkers Police Department, and Higgins for saving their lives from the freezing water. 'I know I don't want to be back in that water. I don't want Deniece to be back in that water,' Smidt told CNN. Smidt and De Priester were taken to Jacobi Medical Center on Sunday and released on Monday. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the cause of the crash. Attempts to reach Smidt and De Priester for comment were unsuccessful. CNN's Mary Snow contributed to this report.

article_content: By Ted Thornhill. PUBLISHED: 06:25 EST, 8 October 2013. | UPDATED: 08:34 EST, 8 October 2013. In a remarkable escape, a seal survived a close encounter with a Great White shark by balancing on its nose â inches from its razor-sharp teeth. Photographer David 'Baz' Jenkins, 41, from Dublin, Ireland, captured the dramatic scene while on a shark-watching tour boat off the coast of Cape Town, South Africa. The seals were returning to Seal Island after feeding at sea when a Great White launched a surprise attack from below. These apex predators are expertly camouflaged by their dark backs, making them nearly invisible against the deep ocean. Great Whites can accelerate upward at speeds of up to 25 mph, launching both themselves and their prey out of the water in a powerful breach. In this instance, the seal managed to evade capture by briefly balancing on the sharkâs snout before darting away. Jenkins noted, 'Iâve seen sharks lose teeth on decoys during mock breaches, but never during an actual hunt. The speed and agility of these animals are breathtaking â they strike without warning.' Great White sharks are the worldâs largest predatory fish, reaching lengths of up to 20 feet and weights of around 5,000 pounds. Their hunting behavior is a vital part of marine ecosystem balance. Though the seal appeared to be doomed, it used its agility and instinct to escape â a rare and awe-inspiring moment caught on camera.

article_content: (CNN) â Remember when social media websites were just about sharing fun moments? Iâm talking about the time when Facebook was mostly a place to post photos of you having a great time, and the most serious update was changing your relationship status from 'in a relationship' to 'single.' Those days are gone. Social media has now become a space for sharing deeply personal â and often painfully difficult â events in our lives. It has, in essence, turned into an online group therapy session, where people reveal intimate details of traumatic experiences in hopes of coping and finding support. We saw this clearly this week with 16-year-old Hannah Anderson, who was held hostage by James DiMaggio for a week after he allegedly killed her mother and younger brother. Shortly after being freed, Hannah went online to ask.fm and answered a long series of public questions about her ordeal â from 'Why didnât you run?' to 'Are you glad DiMaggio is dead?' I first noticed this shift in how people used social media last year, and at the time, I wasnât comfortable with it. My concern: Why would anyone share the most intimate details of tragedy with strangers online? It hit home this year when a friend posted on Facebook that heâd been diagnosed with cancer. I was stunned â not just by the news, but by the fact he announced it publicly on Facebook. Usually, this kind of news is shared face-to-face with close family and friends. But reading the comments on his posts â and the ongoing responses to his updates about treatment â changed my perspective. The outpouring of support was overwhelming. He told me it gave him comfort and motivated him to fight harder. Others are doing the same. In recent weeks, friends have shared news of parents or grandparents passing away. This week, I saw someone post that his brother in Egypt had been shot by police during protests. Hours later, he updated with news of emergency surgery. Finally, he shared a photo of his brotherâs body from the morgue. A few weeks ago, NPR host Scott Simon live-tweeted from his motherâs hospital room as she died, reaching over a million followers. Critics called it an invasion of privacy or self-indulgence. But to me, it felt like a profound, honest tribute. Whatâs driving this trend? First, itâs therapeutic. Sharing pain helps some people heal â and the support they receive strengthens them. Second, people whoâve used social media daily for years have grown accustomed to sharing everything â from meals to milestones â so now theyâre extending that openness to grief and trauma. Third, I believe reality TV has normalized this behavior. For over a decade, weâve watched strangers pour out their triumphs and tragedies on shows like 'Big Brother,' 'The Real World,' 'Honey Boo Boo,' and 'Keeping Up with the Kardashians.' Itâs made vulnerability feel less taboo. The best part? You control it. Itâs your choice whether to share. Those who find it uncomfortable can stay silent. But for many, social media offers a low-cost, accessible form of emotional support.

As the supernatural threat grows, she must race against time to save her rebellious teenage daughter from being consumed by the entity's curse. Joining Burrows are veteran actors James Cosmo and Toby Stephens, lending depth to this mythologically rich tale. Written and directed by Colum Eastwood â who previously crafted the short film that inspired this feature â 'The Morrigan' is brought to life by producers Ashley Holberry and Gavin Cosmo Mehrtens under their company Cowboy Cosmonaut Films. Backed by Quickfire Films, Northern Ireland Screen, M2 Mediapost, and private investors, the project operates under a SAG-AFTRA interim agreement. Global sales rights are being handled by AMP, which is pitching the film at the upcoming American Film Market. According to AMPâs James Norrie, the movie revitalizes the possession genre by merging raw horror with a powerful mother-daughter bond rooted in Celtic legend. article_content: On December 20, 2013, a Robinson R44 helicopter crashed into the Dordogne River in southwestern France, killing all four people on board. The victims were Chinese billionaire Lam Kok, 46; his 12-year-old son, Shun Yu Kok; interpreter Peng Wang; and French winemaker James Gregoire, the former owner of ChÃ¢teau de la RiviÃ¨re. The group had just finalized the purchase of the historic 160-acre estate and were embarking on a brief celebratory flight over the vineyard when the aircraft disappeared. Emergency teams recovered the wreckage using a crane, and the body of Shun Yu Kok was retrieved. Searches for the other three continued under difficult conditions: freezing water, strong river currents, and almost no visibility. James Gregoire, who had acquired the estate in 2003 after its previous owner, Jean Leprince, died in a similar helicopter crash in 2002, was believed to be piloting the aircraft. Lam Kokâs wife had chosen not to join the flight at the last minute, saying she was afraid of helicopters. Lam Kokâs company, Brilliant Group â based in Hong Kong and specializing in rare teas like Pu'er and luxury hotels â planned to transform the chÃ¢teau into a high-end tea and wine tasting center. This acquisition reflected a broader trend of Chinese investors purchasing French vineyards, though most deals had previously been under â¬10 million. The price of this sale was not disclosed. More than 100 police officers, divers, infrared-equipped helicopters, and specialized sonar equipment from Strasbourg were deployed in the search. Authorities stated that determining the cause of the crash could take weeks or months, and no evidence of foul play had been found.

article_content: The grieving parents of a stillborn baby were devastated to learn they had buried the wrong infant following a mix-up at Brookside Funeral Home in Houston. Mercedez Uscanga and her partner Robert Mares had said a heartfelt farewell to their first son, Armani Angel Mares, during a funeral service last week. 'They called and told us that my baby is still at the funeral home,' Uscanga told ABC13. The couple realized the infant interred in the casket was not their sonâArmani remained in the morgue. 'We were crying for our baby,' Uscanga said, 'and we didnât even know. We thought our baby was the one in the casket.' The family quickly arranged for another funeral home to retrieve Armani. His grandfather, George Uscanga, expressed profound shock: 'Iâm speechless. Iâm speechless.' The couple is now consulting an attorney and demanding a formal investigation into the error. Brookside Memorial Park responded by saying they are working closely with the family to resolve the matter. 'Out of respect for the privacy of the families, it would be inappropriate to release any details,' the funeral home stated. 'We have policies and procedures in place; however, occasionally mistakes happen. In those instances, we maintain full disclosure with the families.'

The official 'Men of the Strip' Twitter account shared a statement: 'Management and the cast of Men of the Strip are extremely saddened by the loss of one of our own. Cast member Nate. We thank you for your heartfelt condolences and expressions of love and support.' Jeff Simmons, founder of the troupe, called Estimada 'a gift to all of us' and said he would be deeply missed both personally and professionally. A planned performance in Minnesota has been rescheduled for August.

article_content: Air India is facing ongoing challenges with rodents boarding its aircraft, with at least four confirmed sightings this year alone. The latest incident occurred when a rat was spotted on a flight arriving from Ranchi to New Delhiâs Indira Gandhi International Airport. The plane was immediately grounded and thoroughly fumigated upon landing, following standard safety procedures. This isnât an isolated case. Earlier this month, crew members on another Air India flight â an Airbus A321 traveling from Kolkata â reported rats moving freely in the rear cabin. That aircraft was also removed from service and moved to a secluded bay for disinfection. In May, a pilot claimed to have seen a rat in the cockpit during a flight to London, though some reports question whether the animal was actually onboard. The airline has faced delays before due to suspected rodent activity â like a two-hour hold in February after a Mumbai-bound flight. Even unverified sightings trigger mandatory fumigation because rats can gnaw through critical wiring and damage electronic systems, potentially endangering lives. These pests usually hitch rides on catering trucks loaded with food supplies. Similar cases have happened globally: in 2023, Chinese inspectors found nearly a dozen rats beneath a business-class seat on a flight from Hong Kong to Xiamen. Crew in full protective gear combed through overhead bins and seat panels to locate them. Back in 2009, an Air India flight from Amritsar to Toronto was delayed for hours while ground staff attempted to capture a rat spotted mid-flight â eventually requiring a replacement plane. Despite advances in aviation hygiene, these incidents show how vulnerable aircraft remain to small but dangerous intruders.

article_content: Jerry Buss, the longtime owner of the Los Angeles Lakers who purchased the team in 1979, died on February 18, 2013, at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. He was 79 years old. News of his passing came just days after reports that he had been hospitalized in intensive care due to cancer. His assistant, Bob Steiner, confirmed that while Buss had been battling cancer, the immediate cause of death was kidney failure. Under Bussâs leadership, the Lakers became Southern Californiaâs most beloved sports franchise and a global symbol of Hollywood glamour. He acquired, nurtured, and befriended an extraordinary roster of players and basketball minds during his Hall of Fame tenure. No other owner in NBA history matched Bussâs achievements: under his 32-year ownership, the Lakers reached the NBA Finals 16 times and won 10 championships between 1980 and 2010 â making them the leagueâs most successful franchise since 1979. Buss was deeply respected by players, often referring to the team as his extended family. Legends such as Kobe Bryant and Magic Johnson visited him in his final days. NBA Commissioner David Stern said: 'The NBA has lost a visionary owner whose influence on our league is incalculable and will be felt for decades to come. More importantly, we have lost a dear and valued friend.' Working closely with executives Jerry West and Mitch Kupchak, Buss spent generously to build championship teams â often maintaining the NBAâs highest payroll despite not possessing a vast personal fortune. He paid top salaries to coaches like Pat Riley and Phil Jackson. A pioneer in sports media, Buss co-founded the Prime Ticket cable network in 1985, bringing Lakers games to basic cable at a time when subscription models dominated. He also sold the naming rights to the Forum â innovations that later became industry standards. He was inducted into the Pro Basketball Hall of Fame in 2010 and received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2006. Bussâs legacy includes the iconic 'Showtime' era of the 1980s, led by Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and James Worthy, and the three-peat championship runs of the early 2000s with Shaquille OâNeal and Kobe Bryant, followed by back-to-back titles in 2009 and 2010 with Bryant and Pau Gasol. Beyond basketball, Buss was a scholar: he earned a Ph.D. in chemistry at age 24 and built a career in aerospace and real estate before entering sports. He used wealth from his Santa Monica real estate ventures to buy the Lakers, the NHLâs Los Angeles Kings, and the Forum in a $67.5 million deal â the largest sports transaction in history at the time. His children, Jim Buss and Jeanie Buss, now lead the franchiseâs basketball and business operations, respectively. Yet Jerry remained actively involved in major decisions, including the 2012 acquisitions of Steve Nash and Dwight Howard, and the coaching changes that brought Mike DâAntoni aboard. Buss was frequently seen with younger women and was known for his vibrant, cosmopolitan lifestyle â embodying California cool. He was hospitalized multiple times in recent years, including for dehydration in 2012 and blood clots in 2011. Forbes estimated the Lakersâ value at $643 million in January 2011 â the second-highest in the NBA.

article_content: Israel has recalled its ambassador to South Africa, Eliav Belotserkovsky, 'for consultations,' according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. The decision follows recent statements by South Africa criticizing Israelâs military operations in Gaza. Spokesperson Lior Haiat made the announcement on X but did not specify the nature of these remarks. On Tuesday, South Africaâs parliament passed a non-binding motion urging the closure of Israelâs embassy until a ceasefire is achieved and peace talks begin. The motion won 248 votes to 91, with full support from the ruling African National Congress. However, it remains uncertain whether the government will implement the recommendation. Amid the vote, some lawmakers chanted 'Free, free Palestine,' despite objections from the presiding officer. Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza following a deadly cross-border assault by Hamas on October 7, which killed at least 1,200 people and took over 200 hostages. Israel says its goal is to dismantle Hamas and prevent future attacks, framing its actions as self-defense. Gazaâs Hamas-run health ministry reports over 13,000 deaths since the start of the Israeli offensive. Meanwhile, U.S. President Joe Biden stated that a deal for the release of some hostages is 'very close.' The recall comes just before South Africa hosts a virtual Brics summit focused on the conflict. At its conclusion, Brics leaders â including China and Russia â called for an immediate and sustained humanitarian truce in Gaza. Chinese President Xi Jinping urged the release of civilian detainees, while Russian President Vladimir Putin accused the United States of obstructing peace efforts. South Africa has formally asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to issue an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by mid-December. Minister Khumbudzo Ntshavheni warned that failure to do so would signify a 'total failure of global governance.' South Africa, alongside Bangladesh, Bolivia, Comoros, and Djibouti, has referred the situation in Gaza to the ICC, alleging possible war crimes and crimes against humanity. The United Nations Security Council has demanded 'urgent and extended humanitarian pauses' lasting several days to allow aid agencies safe access to Gaza. South Africa previously recalled its own ambassador from Israel earlier this month and has not had a resident ambassador there for five years.

article_content: A rare deck of 52 playing cards, each featuring an intricately hand-drawn map of an English or Welsh county, is set to be auctioned by Sothebyâs. Though visually suited for games, these cards are far too valuable â estimated at Â£4,500 â to be used at a poker table. Created in 1676 by renowned cartographer Robert Morden, each card displays a detailed map of its respective county, including major cities, roads, and the distance to London. The top-left corner indicates the suit, while the top-right shows the cardâs rank â number or face. The King is depicted as Charles II, the reigning monarch at the time; the Queen is Catherine of Braganza, his wife. The Jacks feature various male portraits. Each card also includes the county name at the top, the card number on the left, and its Roman numeral equivalent on the right. Additional data such as width, breadth, and circumference of each county are inscribed on the cards, enhancing their cartographic value. These were not designed primarily for gambling, but as decorative and educational objects â a novelty for collectors and map enthusiasts. The earliest known map-based playing cards were produced in 1590 by William Bowes. However, those featured only rudimentary green-ink outlines of counties, lacking roads, cities, or detailed geographic data. Bowesâs deck included four introductory cards depicting Elizabeth Iâs royal arms, her portrait, a map of England and Wales, and a birdâs-eye view of London, alongside four text-only cards describing Englandâs history and governance. During the Puritan era under Oliver Cromwell, playing cards were deemed sinful and many were destroyed. This explains the scarcity of early examples. This 1676 deck was once owned by Jaime âJimmyâ Ortiz-Patino, former president of the World Bridge Federation and founder of Spainâs famed Valderrama Golf Course. It will be offered at auction next week.

That same year, workers claimed to hear the sound of a spinning wheel coming through a wall â leading to the discovery of a hidden chamber containing an antique wheel. Legend says her spirit still wanders the halls. Though the palace suffered major damage in a 1986 fire, its reputation as one of Britainâs most haunted sites endures.

article_content: Adnan el Shukrijumah, chief of global operations for Al-Qaeda, was killed in a raid by the Pakistani military this morning. The military confirmed that Shukrijumah, an Al-Qaeda leader accused of planning attacks on the London Underground and New York Metro, was eliminated alongside two other suspected militants in Shinwarsak, South Waziristan. He had been hiding in a compound after fleeing from North Waziristan, where the Pakistani army launched a major offensive against militant bases in June. 'The Al-Qaeda leader killed in this successful operation is the same individual indicted in the United States,' said a senior Pakistani army officer. Shukrijumah, who lived in the U.S. for 15 years, was accused of involvement in plots targeting the London Underground and trains in Norwayânone of which were carried out. He assumed a leadership role previously held by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the mastermind behind the September 11 attacks, who was captured in 2003. U.S. federal prosecutors allege that in 2008, Shukrijumah recruited three men to receive terrorist training in Pakistanâs tribal regions for planned attacks. The New York indictment connects him to a failed plot to bomb the Manhattan subway system and a similar scheme targeting British underground rail lines. A Â£3.2 million reward had been offered for information leading to his capture. Pakistani military spokesman Major General Asim Bajwa stated on Twitter that five additional terrorists were arrested during the operation. After the September 11 attacks, captured Al-Qaeda member Abu Zubaydah told U.S. authorities that Shukrijumah was considered one of the groupâs most viable assets for launching attacks inside the U.S. or Europe. Shukrijumah studied at a community college in Florida, but fled the country before the FBI could arrest him as a material witness in a terrorism case in 2003. U.S. officials believe he traveled through Trinidad and London before reaching Al-Qaeda camps in Afghanistan, where he began in low-level roles. The FBI had been seeking Shukrijumah since 2003 but elevated him to the top of its wanted list after three men accused of plotting subway bombings in New York last year identified him as their key liaison in Pakistan.

article_content: Tiger Woods is set to make his return to the PGA Tour this Thursday after a three-month absence, but this time without his longtime caddie, Steve Williams. His comeback comes at the World Golf Championships-Bridgestone Invitational in Akron, Ohio â a tournament he has won a record seven times â following recovery from knee and Achilles injuries. Speaking after a practice round on Tuesday, Woods said he felt fitter than he had in years and experienced no pain following surgery on his left leg. 'It feels solid, it feels stable, no pain,' he said. 'Thatâs one of the reasons I waited so long to return â I wanted to reach this point, where I can play golf again without limitations.' 'Itâs been a very long time,' he added. 'It feels good to be out here, hitting balls, practicing, walking the course â doing everything I want without discomfort.' This marks his first tournament since parting ways with Williams, who caddied for him for 12 years. When asked about the split â amid reports that Williams felt heâd 'wasted the past two years' â Woods acknowledged their successful partnership. 'Heâs a hell of a caddie, no doubt. He helped my career, and I think I helped his too. Weâve won a lot together over 12 years. But I just felt it was time for a change.' Woods will tee off at 1:40 p.m. at Firestone Country Club, with friend Bryon Bell as his new caddie. He withdrew from the PLAYERS Championship in May due to his left knee injury and a strained Achilles tendon, and subsequently missed both the U.S. Open in June and the British Open in July. The 35-year-old golfer, who won the British Open in 2000, 2005, and 2006, also missed the 2008 edition after undergoing reconstructive knee surgery following his U.S. Open victory. Since his personal scandal broke in late 2009 â leading to his divorce from wife Elin Nordegren in August 2010 â Woods has not won a professional tournament.

article_content: OpenAI has rolled out two major upgrades to ChatGPT: voice interaction and image understandingâfeatures currently exclusive to ChatGPT Plus subscribers. Starting in late September, paying users can now speak naturally to the AI and receive spoken replies, turning conversations into something closer to chatting with a person. They can also snap or upload photos and ask questions about themâwhether itâs deciphering messy handwriting, identifying a struggling houseplant, or even translating a hand-drawn whiteboard sketch into functional code. On desktop, a simple camera icon beside the text box lets users drag and drop images. Mobile users can take a photo directly through the app and draw circles around specific elements to focus the AIâs attention. One tester fed it a jumble of pantry items and got four plausible recipes within minutesâeven suggesting ingredients not visible in the photo. Another used it to convert scribbled notes into clean digital text and received care tips for a wilting succulent. But the real showstopper? A developer named Mckay Wrigley demonstrated how ChatGPT could turn a hand-drawn wireframe of a website into working HTML and JavaScriptâjust by analyzing the image. Itâs a glimpse into how AI might soon replace sketch-to-code workflows entirely. Still, caution is advised. Security experts like Reece Rogers from Wired warn against uploading private photosâthink ID cards, passports, or family snapshotsâsince the system stores inputs to improve performance. OpenAI has added safeguards: the bot refuses to name people in photos unless thereâs a clear label nearby. When shown a portrait of Frida Kahlo, it initially declined to identify herâ¦ until prompted to examine the tiny signature in the corner. 'Iâm designed to protect privacy,' it explained. 'But since this image is labeled, I can confirm itâs Frida Kahlo.'

article_content: By Reuters and the Associated Press. PUBLISHED: 02:00 EST, 24 December 2013 | UPDATED: 02:15 EST, 24 December 2013. Pope Francis visited Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI on Monday and said he found his 86-year-old predecessor looking well, according to television footage released by the Vatican. Francis, elected in March 2013, spent approximately 30 minutes with Benedict at the Mater Ecclesiae monastery, an ex-convent on Vatican grounds where the former pope has lived in quiet seclusion since his resignation. Photos published by LâOsservatore Romano, the Vatican newspaper, show both men dressed in identical white cassocks â except for Francisâ red cape â conversing in Benedictâs sitting room. They also prayed together in the adjacent chapel. 'Itâs a pleasure to see you looking so well,' Francis told Benedict, who in February 2013 became the first pope in nearly 600 years to resign rather than serve for life. The footage â only the fourth time Benedict has been filmed since stepping down â showed him alert and in better health than in prior appearances. He used a cane for support while standing in prayer. This marked the first public glimpse inside Benedictâs residence. The sitting room and furnishings were entirely white, with an Advent wreath on the coffee table. Since Benedictâs resignation on February 28, 2013, the two have met only once publicly â at an official Vatican ceremony in July â but have maintained private contact, including occasional phone calls. Benedict greeted Francis at the door of his residence, leaning on an ivory-handled wooden cane. They walked to the chapel, stood in silent prayer, then spoke privately in another room. As Francis departed, he said, 'Merry Christmas â pray for me.' Benedict replied, 'Always, always, always.' Benedict resigned citing diminished physical and spiritual strength to lead the 1.2 billion-member Roman Catholic Church.

article_content: The United Nations is calling on nations to invest in green jobs centered around sustainable forest management as a solution to rising global unemployment. According to an upcoming report by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), up to 10 million such jobs could be created worldwide. The report, while not naming specific countries, targets regions with high levels of rural unemployment and degraded landâparticularly in Asia, Africa, and to a lesser extent, Latin America. C.T.S. Nair, Chief Economist at the UN Forestry Department and co-author of the report, noted that countries like India, China, and nearly all African nations stand to gain significantly. Sustainable forestry seeks to prevent deforestation by ensuring responsible harvesting: workers are employed to monitor timber extraction, protect biodiversity, and safeguard water supplies. These efforts allow forests to regenerate naturally while supporting local livelihoods. The FAO will present the findings next week at the UN Committee on Forestry meeting in Rome, Italy, which coincides with World Forest Week.

article_content: The 12th Duke of Marlborough led mourners at the funeral of his father, the 11th Duke, John Spencer-Churchill, at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire. Jamie Blandford, 58, formerly the Marquess of Blandford, walked arm in arm with his stepmother, Lily Mahtani â his fatherâs fourth wife â as they followed the coffin, carried by estate gamekeepers in traditional plus fours, into St Mary Magdalene Church in Woodstock. Uniformed palace staff and estate workers bowed their heads as the horse-drawn carriage passed through the 11,500-acre parkland en route to the private service. A flag bearing the Marlborough crest flew at half-mast over the UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the formal gardens were closed for the occasion. The 11th Duke died last Thursday at age 88, just over a week before the funeral. Hundreds of locals and tourists lined the streets of Woodstock to witness the procession. Inside the church, the new Duke delivered a reading, joined by his siblings â Lady Alexandra, Lord Edward, and Lady Henrietta Spencer-Churchill â as well as Sir Mark Weinberg and Rev Canon Adrian Daffern, who described the Duke as 'a man of authority, tempered by his humanity' who deeply loved the estate and the county. After the service, the 12th Duke led the funeral party on foot back to Blenheim Palace. Though the private ceremony concluded, the park remained open to the public, with entrance fees waived so visitors could pay their respects. The 11th Duke married four times: first to Susan Hornby, heiress of WHSmith, mother of his first three children; then to Athina Onassis; then to Rosita Douglas-Sjernorp, mother of his three younger children; and finally to Persian-born Lily Mahtani. His four surviving children are Jamie (now the 12th Duke), Lady Henrietta (56), Lord Edward (40), and Lady Alexandra (38). Jamie Blandford had been estranged from his father for over two decades due to battles with drug addiction and multiple prison sentences, which prompted the 11th Duke to take legal steps to protect the estate. Their reconciliation in 2008 â widely attributed to Lily Mahtaniâs quiet efforts â marked a turning point. Blandford and his wife, ceramicist Edla Griffiths, moved onto the estate, where he took over management of the Blenheim farm shop. Blenheim Palace, built in the 18th century as a gift from Queen Anne to John Churchill, the 1st Duke of Marlborough, commemorates his victory over Louis XIV. It is the birthplace of Sir Winston Churchill and now houses 187 rooms â a vast estate that, while smaller than Buckingham Palace, remains one of Britainâs most impressive historic homes. The estate draws around half a million visitors annually. Legend holds that Adolf Hitler ordered the Luftwaffe to spare it during WWII, intending to reside there after a hypothetical invasion of Britain â though this claim lacks documented evidence. The 12th Duke now inherits the estate, continuing his fatherâs lifelong mission to preserve it. Among the mourners were Viscount Linley, billionaire Arpad Busson, Conservative MP Sir Nicholas Soames, Lady Forte, energy entrepreneur Algy Cluff, and the 12th Dukeâs first wife, Becky Few Brown. The coffin, draped in the family flag and adorned with white roses and lilies, was carried by gamekeepers in plus fours â a symbolic nod to tradition.

article_content: Tuesday night brought the debut of three new TV showsâFoxâs 'The Mindy Project,' Foxâs 'Ben & Kate,' and CBSâs 'Vegas'âall fighting for attention in packed prime-time slots. While 'The Mindy Project' kicked off with 4.7 million viewers and a 2.4 demo rating, it slipped 23% compared to last yearâs 'Raising Hope' premiere. Still, it managed to beat NBCâs 'The New Normal' (5.2 million, 2.0) in its 9:30 p.m. timeslot. Meanwhile, 'Ben & Kate' struggled from the start, pulling in just 4.2 million viewers at 8:30 p.m., despite benefiting from the same lead-in as 'The Mindy Project.' That lead-in? A special encore of 'New Girl' at 8 p.m., which drew 5.3 million viewers, followed by its official 9 p.m. debut at 5.2 millionâthe same demo score as the earlier episode, though both were down 44% from last yearâs premiere. Interestingly, the 9 p.m. 'New Girl' tied with NBCâs 'Go On,' starring Matthew Perry, which held steady despite a slight dip. On the drama front, CBSâs 'Vegas' delivered a surprising 14.7 million total viewersâthe largest CBS Tuesday drama premiere audience since 2002âbut its 2.5 demo rating was the weakest since 2004, suggesting it attracted mostly older viewers. This disconnect makes 'Vegas' a head-scratcher: record-breaking in one metric, historic in another. Elsewhere, CBS ruled the night thanks to 'NCIS' (20.2 million, 4.1) and 'NCIS: LA' (16.7 million, 3.4), both holding strong. NBCâs 'The Voice' dipped 15% to 11.3 million, while 'Parenthood' stayed flat at 4.8 million. ABCâs 'Dancing With the Stars' continued its slump, falling 31% to 11.6 million, and 'Private Practice' lost ground after moving from Thursday, dropping 32% to 6.6 million. Though none of the new shows exploded, their numbers werenât disastrous. Sitcoms often find their footing over time, while dramas like 'Vegas' may need to win over younger viewers to survive. Next weekâs ratings will tell us if these shows are here to stayâor just passing through.

article_content: Refusing to give up: Naked Rambler Stephen Gough, 54, has lost his case at the European Court of Human Rights. Judges ruled that Britain's best-known naturist cannot avoid arrest for walking naked in public. Gough, a former marine, has spent more than five years in jails and police cells for refusing to wear clothing â insisting his treatment violated his fundamental rights. He was repeatedly jailed for contempt of court after appearing naked in courtrooms, and further isolated in prison for refusing to wear clothes even behind bars. He appealed to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, arguing that police and prison officials violated his rights to freedom of expression and private life. Today, the court sided with the UK government in both cases. While acknowledging the case was 'troubling,' the court emphasized that Gough had 'full knowledge of the consequences' when he began his naked treks. His behavior, it stated, 'goes against the standards of accepted public behaviour in any modern democratic society' and is 'alarming and morally offensive.' Gough has walked naked from John OâGroats to Landâs End and is a well-known campaigner for the right to appear nude in public. Between May 2006 and July 2011, he was detained for a total of five years and three months, sparking his human rights appeal. The ruling, led by Latvian court president Ineta Ziemele, concludes a long legal battle. Gough described the decision as 'a disappointment' but vowed to continue: 'I have no choice but to continue.' He was awarded â¬3,000 (Â£2,360) in damages for distress caused by the physical conditions of his detention â far less than the â¬195,000 (Â£154,000) he sought. Even in prison, Gough was often segregated because he refused guardsâ offers of clothing. In 2009, court officials erected a screen around his private parts to avoid contempt of court. In 2011, he walked out of Perth Prison naked and was arrested within minutes â still refusing to dress. At his final hearing, he pleaded not guilty to breaching the peace, ignoring the sheriffâs warnings. The court found his conduct severely alarmed the public, threatened community order, and was genuinely shocking in context. He received a combined sentence of one year, nine months, and 18 days. Gough questioned: 'How can nature expressed in human form be indecent? How can any sane person be offended at seeing the human body?' He added: 'Intolerance and ignorance go together... We cannot be intolerant and free. We cannot ignore the truth and expect justice to be the outcome.' Despite the ruling, Gough remains undeterred: 'I was brought up to believe I lived in a country that celebrated eccentricity and difference â not because it was quirky, but because true freedom thrives on originality.'

article_content: Thousands of women migrant domestic workers in Qatar are enduring severe exploitation and sexual abuse under conditions described by Amnesty International as 'utterly miserable.' A 77-page report, titled 'My sleep is my break: Exploitation of domestic workers in Qatar,' reveals that womenâprimarily from the Philippines, Indonesia, and Sri Lankaâare lured to Qatar with false promises of fair wages and decent working conditions. Instead, they are forced to work up to 100 hours per week, seven days a week, with no days off. Under Qatari law, domestic workers have no legal protections: there are no limits on working hours, no mandatory rest periods, and no formal channel to file complaints with the Labour Ministry. These workers are trapped under the kafala sponsorship system, which requires employer approval to change jobs or leave the country. Many have their passports and mobile phones confiscated, isolating them completely. Some women report physical and sexual violenceâincluding being slapped, kicked, pulled by the hair, poked in the eyes, and even raped. In one horrific case, a woman broke both legs and fractured her spine trying to escape a rape attempt. Her attacker sexually assaulted her while she lay injured on the ground before calling an ambulance. Six months later, she was still in a wheelchair. Despite clear evidence, Qatarâs public prosecutor dismissed her case for 'lack of evidence.' Her employer was never held accountable. Women who flee abusive homes are labeled 'runaways' and face arrest, detention, and deportation. Those who report sexual abuse risk being criminally charged for extramarital sexâa punishable offense in Qatar. One worker, identified as PD, was promised $400 monthly but received only $247. When she complained, her employer told her, 'You donât deserve it.' She worked from 4 a.m. with only three to four hours of sleep, suffered bleeding hands from constant labor, and was denied bathroom breaks. Recruitment agencies, instead of helping, pressured her to stay. 'They stopped answering the phone,' she said. Amnesty Internationalâs Audrey Gaughran stated that the isolation of domestic workers in private homes makes them especially vulnerable to abuse, calling the system 'discriminatory' and 'ripe for forced labor and human trafficking.' Promises by Qatari authorities to reform labor protections have so far yielded no tangible results.

article_content: A Minnesota doctor, Dr. Stephen Larson, 74, of Orono, may have been shot and killed last week by Ted Hoffstrom, 30, a man he delivered at birth in 1983. Hoffstrom, a recent law school graduate, reportedly blamed Larson for a congenital hand condition he believed resulted from complications during his delivery. Former classmates at the University of St. Thomas told Fox Twin Cities that Hoffstrom had longstanding difficulties with fine motor skills in his hands and attributed them to his birth experience. Hennepin County Sheriff Rich Stanek confirmed that Dr. Larson had assisted in Hoffstromâs birth but declined to discuss any specific medical details due to privacy laws. According to authorities, Hoffstrom had recently expressed hostility toward Dr. Larson to family members. On Friday evening, police responded to reports of an armed man outside Larsonâs home on Heritage Lane. After shots were fired, Hoffstrom was killed by officers outside the residence. Dr. Larson was found deceased inside the home. Colleagues at OBGYN Specialists described Larson as a dedicated physician with a 33-year career who delivered thousands of babies and received numerous awards. One partner, Dr. Suzin Cho, stated, 'There is no way anyone would have ill will toward him.' Hoffstrom had recently passed the Minnesota bar exam, according to the St. Paul Pioneer Press. His family released a statement expressing profound grief, calling the shooting 'shocking and out of character,' and asked the public to respect their privacy during this difficult time. A handwritten note left on the familyâs front door read: 'We are grieving the loss of our son. Please respect our privacy.'

article_content: Leaked screenshots suggest the next major version of Google's Android operating system will feature a significant visual redesign â adopting a 'flat' icon style reminiscent of Apple's iOS 7. The new interface appears to align more closely with Google's existing web aesthetics, moving away from the previously used 3D-style icons. According to Android Police, which published the images, the upcoming update â internally rumored to be called 'Moonshine' â will refresh launcher icons to match the minimalist style seen across Google's web platforms. The update is also expected to deepen integration between Chrome and Android. This shift echoes Appleâs controversial yet highly successful transition from skeuomorphic to flat design under lead designer Sir Jonathan Ive. Appleâs former head of iOS software, Scott Forstall, had championed skeuomorphism â using realistic textures like leather, wood, and felt in apps such as Find My Friends, iBooks, and Game Center. Critics found these designs outdated and cluttered. Forstall was removed from his role in late 2012 following the poor reception of Apple Maps and underperformance in quarterly earnings. His departure coincided with Ive assuming leadership over Human Interface design, signaling a bold new direction for Appleâs software. Now, Google appears to be following a similar path. While experts initially warned users might find Appleâs radical redesign confusing, iOS 7 went on to achieve record adoption rates. Google is anticipated to unveil the new Android interface at its I/O developer conference in San Francisco in June.

article_content: By Anna Hodgekiss. PUBLISHED: 04:46 EST, 17 April 2013. | UPDATED: 07:39 EST, 17 April 2013. A 78-year-old woman, Joan Smith, suffered a heart attack upstairs in her home in Hull. Each time paramedics attempted to carry her downstairs on a stretcher, her heart stopped. Recognizing that keeping her completely horizontal was essential for her survival, they determined the only viable option was to use an aerial ladder platform to extract her through the bedroom window. Fire crews arrived to position the crane, and Mrs. Smith was carefully lifted out of the window onto the platform and lowered to the ground. During the procedure, she required two rounds of resuscitation as paramedics fought to maintain her vital signs. Her husband, Brian Smith, said: 'Without doubt, the emergency crews saved my wifeâs life. They were absolutely marvellous â I couldnât ask for more.' He recalled finding her collapsed, unresponsive but staring at him. 'I called 999 immediately.' Emergency teams maintained her horizontal position throughout the rescue, as upright movement threatened to worsen her condition. Once on the ground, she was rushed to the hospital, where doctors inserted a line through her neck to support circulation. She was expected to undergo surgery to receive a pacemaker. Steve Johnson, clinical supervisor at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, said: 'The patient suffered a life-threatening condition that made movement extremely dangerous. The first responders stabilized her, but it quickly became clear we needed to keep her as flat as possible.' Crowds gathered below as crews worked urgently to transfer her into the waiting ambulance.

article_content: In a rare and unexpected medical event, a woman in Bellflower, California, gave birth to eight healthy premature babies â the second known instance of live-born octuplets in the United States. Doctors preparing for a septuplet delivery were stunned when an eighth infant emerged during the C-section. The newborns, born at just 23 weeks gestation, range in weight from just over a pound to just over three pounds. Six are boys and two are girls. Though three need help breathing, none show signs of life-threatening complications, according to medical staff at Kaiser Permanente Hospital. The delivery, which lasted only five minutes, was the result of weeks of meticulous planning by a team of 46 healthcare professionals. Dr. Karen Maples, head of obstetrics, called it 'a truly amazing delivery.' Dr. Harold Henry noted that spotting all eight babies on ultrasound beforehand was extremely difficult â missing one when expecting seven isnât uncommon. The mother, whose name and medical history remain private, is recovering well and reportedly thrilled with the outcome. The infants are expected to stay in the NICU for up to eight weeks and may remain hospitalized for as long as 10 weeks. The only prior recorded case of live-born octuplets in the U.S. occurred in Houston in 1998; one of those babies passed away shortly after birth, while the other seven recently turned 10.

article_content: In Rio de Janeiro, a peaceful teachers' strike demanding fair wages turned chaotic when thousands of demonstratorsâteachers, students, and activistsâclashed with police near City Hall. What began as a quiet march through Cinelandia Square spiraled into disorder after protesters confronted legislation that weakened their working conditions. Some individuals, many masked, hurled firebombs, stones, and tear gas canisters at law enforcement. One bus was set ablaze, and bank doors were forced open, with attackers attempting to destroy or steal from ATMs. Police retaliated with tear gas, prompting demonstrators to drag furniture into the streets and build barricades. Hugo Cryois, a 23-year-old anarchist wearing a gas mask, told the BBC: 'Thereâs no violence without police. They bring it wherever they go.' While organizers estimated 50,000 people took part, authorities put the number closer to 10,000. The unrest echoes earlier protests in June, when citizens in Belo Horizonte railed against billions spent on World Cup infrastructure while schools and hospitals remained under-resourced. 'We donât need the World Cup,' said 19-year-old Leonardo Fabri. 'We need real education and humane policing.' Indigenous participants joined the rally, their faces painted or masked, symbolizing a broader call for dignity and justice.

article_content: Three lionsâIvan, Cornel, and Lepaâhave been rescued from a private roadside zoo in Novi Pazar, Serbia, and relocated to the Lionsrock Big Cats Sanctuary in South Africa. The lions were originally taken from Belgrade Zoo in 2009 by a private owner, but their continued possession became illegal after Serbia enacted legislation in 2010 banning the private ownership of dangerous wild animals. The operation was led by Four Paws, a London-based international animal welfare organization, in cooperation with Serbiaâs CITES management and enforcement authority. On Saturday, a Four Paws team traveled to Belgrade to oversee final preparations. The lions were transported to Frankfurt Airport, where they boarded a flight bound for Johannesburg. article_content: Washington (CNN) â As Democratic Sen. Mary Landrieu defends her U.S. Senate seat in Louisiana, a new CNN/ORC International poll shows the three-term incumbent holding a narrow lead over her closest Republican rival in the November general election. But in Louisiana, the electoral system adds complexity: nine candidates â Republicans, Democrats, and a Libertarian â are on the ballot. If no candidate surpasses the 50% threshold, the top two finishers advance to a December runoff. Landrieu currently leads with 43% support among likely voters, while Republican Rep. Bill Cassidy stands at 40%. However, the pollâs margin of error is Â±4 percentage points, meaning the two are statistically tied. In a state with deep conservative roots, Landrieu is considered one of the most vulnerable Democratic incumbents this cycle. Republicans, aiming to regain Senate control, view this race as a prime opportunity to pick up a seat â needing a net gain of six to achieve a majority. If the current polling holds, Landrieu and Cassidy would face off in December. Polls suggest Cassidy holds a slight advantage in a two-way matchup: 50% to 47%. 'The December electorate will likely be smaller and demographically distinct from Novemberâs,' said CNN Polling Director Keating Holland. 'Our likely voter model estimates November turnout, but Decemberâs participation will be critical.' Landrieu has emphasized her role as chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlighting benefits to Louisianaâs oil industry. Like other moderate Democrats in conservative states, she has distanced herself from President Barack Obama, whose approval rating in Louisiana stands at just 40%. Instead, she promotes her bipartisan record and independent voting pattern. Yet she has faced negative headlines this fall, including scrutiny over her residency and misuse of taxpayer-funded travel. Republicans, including Cassidy, have amplified a recent photo of Landrieu assisting a LSU fan with a keg stand at a tailgate party. Cassidy, a physician and three-term congressman known for opposing Obamacare, is positioning healthcare reform as a central issue. He seeks to portray Landrieu as a loyalist to Obamaâs agenda. Despite these challenges, Landrieu maintains a significant fundraising edge: $14 million compared to Cassidyâs $8.6 million, according to the Center for Responsive Politics. Democratic outside groups have spent nearly six times more than Republican-aligned organizations. Landrieu dominates in urban areas and among non-white voters (85%), but struggles in suburban districts. Women support her by a narrow margin â 48% to 45% â a smaller gap than typically seen for Democratic female incumbents. The poll was conducted by ORC International via telephone with 1,013 adult Americans from September 22 to 25, 2014.
